question:
Patient note:
A 72-year-old retired shipyard welder with long-standing emphysematous COPD, ischaemic cardiomyopathy (ejection fraction 35 % on an outpatient echocardiogram five months earlier), and stage-3 chronic kidney disease whose outpatient creatinine has hovered near 1.3 mg/dL was brought in from a skilled-nursing facility after a night of progressive dyspnoea and fever that culminated in a brief syncopal spell while he was being transferred from bed to chair for morning hygiene. Facility staff, who are equipped only with basic respiratory aides, reported that the patient had been using his home portable oxygen concentrator set at 2 L/min until midnight, but by 03:00 he was unable to complete sentences, and saturation on their finger probe read 78 % despite escalation to 6 L/min via simple mask. Because the facility has a standing protocol against field intubation unless airway reflexes are lost, the nurse fitted a full-face non-invasive circuit delivering continuous distending pressure of 12 cmH₂O through a turbine unit; an in-line analyzer connected to the wall blender recorded an inspired oxygen fraction of 0.57, and this configuration accompanied him in the ambulance. He remained spontaneously breathing throughout the twenty-minute transport, never received a paralytic or sedative, and no bag-mask ventilation was attempted. Intravenous access consisted of a single 18-gauge cannula through which only a keep-open rate of normal saline ran; no vasopressors, bronchodilators, or antibiotics were begun en route. On arrival to the emergency department—and before any hospital-based therapy was initiated—he was found seated upright on the stretcher, leaning into the mask cushion with visible sternocleidomastoid recruitment, respiratory rate 32/min, pursed-lip expiration, and coarse inspiratory crackles over the right lower thorax. Skin was pale and clammy, capillary refill was delayed at roughly four seconds, and radial pulse was thready. Oscillometric blood pressure on intake was 92/50 mm Hg, heart rate 124 beats/min in an irregularly irregular rhythm matching his known atrial fibrillation, and an oral temperature of 38.6 °C was documented. A left radial arterial catheter was placed within three minutes; the first sample, obtained while mask settings were unchanged, revealed pH 7.29, PaCO₂ 48 mm Hg, bicarbonate 22 mEq/L, lactate 3.8 mmol/L, and a markedly reduced PaO₂ of 59 mm Hg on the aforementioned 57 % inspired oxygen. Neurological check prior to any analgesia showed pupils 3 mm brisk, eyes opening to spoken name, confused conversation in which he supplied the wrong month but his own name, and localisation to trapezius pinch with both arms, yielding a Glasgow Coma Score of 12; no focal deficit in power or tone was appreciated. Cardiovascular examination disclosed a gallop over the apex, no new murmurs, and jugular veins that were difficult to appreciate because of laboured breathing; extremities were cool to touch and mottled to the mid-shin. The abdomen was soft, non-distended, with mild epigastric tenderness but no guarding. A 16-French Foley catheter inserted during the primary survey produced 40 mL of dark amber urine; review of the nursing-home intake-output sheet confirmed only 700 mL over the preceding twenty-four hours. Laboratory studies drawn simultaneously with the arterial sample—before any crystalloid bolus, antimicrobial, or vasoactive drug—showed white-blood-cell count 18.7 × 10³/µL with 13 % band forms, haemoglobin 11.9 g/dL, haematocrit 36 %, and platelet concentration 138 000 /µL. Serum chemistry returned sodium 128 mmol/L, potassium 5.2 mmol/L, chloride 94 mmol/L, an anion gap of 17, glucose 164 mg/dL, blood urea nitrogen 46 mg/dL, and creatinine 2.0 mg/dL—an acute rise from baseline. Liver profile demonstrated aspartate aminotransferase 68 U/L, alanine aminotransferase 60 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 176 U/L, total bilirubin 1.85 mg/dL with predominantly conjugated fraction, and an international normalised ratio of 1.4. Cardiac troponin I was 0.04 ng/mL (indeterminate), C-reactive protein exceeded 200 mg/L, and procalcitonin was 7.1 ng/mL. A portable anteroposterior chest radiograph, obtained while he remained on the non-invasive circuit, demonstrated dense consolidation of the right middle and lower lobes with air bronchograms and a small parapneumonic effusion; the end of the nasogastric tube placed days prior in the facility was seen below the diaphragm, and mediastinal contours were stable. Focused bedside ultrasound revealed a small, vigorously contracting left ventricle, collapsible inferior vena cava measuring 1.0 cm, and no pericardial effusion; lung windows confirmed hepatization of the right lower lobe consistent with lobar pneumonia. Electrocardiography printed just after line placement showed atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response at 122 beats/min, occasional premature ventricular complexes, and nonspecific ST-T wave flattening but no acute ischaemic changes. Up to the moment these data were captured, he had not been exposed to any intravenous fluid bolus, pressor agent, antimicrobial, or corticosteroid, remained unsupported by an endotracheal tube or invasive ventilator, continued to require continuous positive airway pressure at 12 cmH₂O with a 57 % oxygen blend, persisted with a systolic pressure no higher than 92 mm Hg in the absence of pharmacologic support, exhibited mild thrombocytopenia, conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia, an acute creatinine elevation with oliguria totaling only 700 mL over twenty-four hours, and demonstrated moderate encephalopathy while struggling against severe right-sided community-acquired pneumonia complicated by early septic physiology.

Question: What is the patient's Sequential Organ Failure Assessment (SOFA) Score?
solution:
The Sequential Organ Failure Assessment (SOFA) sums six organ-system scores, each graded 0–4. Using the admission findings:
- Respiratory: PaO₂/FiO₂ = 59/0.57 ≈ 104 mm Hg. This is ≥100 but <200 while receiving respiratory support by CPAP: 3.
- Coagulation: Platelets 138,000/µL fall in the 100,000 to <150,000 range: 1.
- Liver: Bilirubin 1.85 mg/dL is ≥1.2 but <2.0: 1.
- Cardiovascular: Mean arterial pressure = (92 + 2 × 50)/3 = 64 mm Hg, below 70 without vasopressors: 1.
- Neurologic: GCS 12 is in the 10–12 range: 2.
- Renal: Creatinine 2.0 mg/dL is in the 2.0–3.4 range: 2. Urine output of 700 mL/24 h does not meet the <500 mL threshold for a higher score.
SOFA = 3 + 1 + 1 + 1 + 2 + 2 = 10.
Final answer: 10
